{{Short description|Spatial correlation coefficient}}
'''Wartenberg's coefficient''' is a measure of correlation developed by epidemiologist [[Daniel Wartenberg]].<ref>{{Cite journal
 | doi = 10.1289/EHP8405
 | first1 = J
 | last1 = Burger
 | first2 = M
 | last2 = Gochfeld
 | year = 2020
 | title = In Memoriam: Daniel Wartenberg (1952–2020)
 | journal = Environ Health Perspect
 | volume = 128
 | issue = 11
 | pages = 111601
 | pmid = 33147071
 | pmc = 7641299
}}</ref> This coefficient is a multivariate extension of spatial autocorrelation that aims to account for spatial dependence of data while studying their [[covariance]].<ref>{{Cite journal
 | doi = 10.1111/j.1538-4632.1985.tb00849.x
 | first1 = D
 | last1 = Wartenberg
 | year = 1985
 | title = Multivariate spatial correlation: a method for exploratory geographical analysis
 | journal = Geographical Analysis
 | volume = 17
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 263–283
| bibcode = 1985GeoAn..17..263W
 }}</ref> A modified version of this statistic is available in the [[R (programming language)|R]] package ''adespatial''.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/adespatial/index.html | title=Adespatial: Multivariate Multiscale Spatial Analysis | date=18 October 2023 }}</ref>

For data <math>x_i</math> measured at <math>N</math> spatial sites [[Moran's I]] is a measure of the spatial  [[autocorrelation]] of the data. By [[Standard score|standardizing]] the observations <math>z_i = (x_i - \bar{x})/s</math> by subtracting the mean and dividing by the variance as well as normalising the spatial weight matrix such that <math>\sum_{ij} w_{ij} = 1</math> we can write Moran's ''I'' as

:<math>I = \sum_{ij} w_{ij} z_i z_j</math>

Wartenberg generalized this by letting <math>z_i</math> be a vector of <math>M</math> observations at <math>i</math> and defining where:
:<math>I = Z^T W Z</math>
* <math>W</math> is the <math>N \times N</math> spatial weight matrix
* <math>Z</math> is the <math>N \times M</math> standardized data matrix
* <math>Z^T</math> is the [[transpose]] of <math>Z</math>
* <math>I</math> is the <math>M \times M</math> spatial correlation matrix.

For two variables <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> the bivariate correlation is
:<math>I_{xy} = \frac{ N \sum_{ij} w_{ij} (x_i - \bar{x}) (y_j - \bar{y})}{ \sqrt{ \sum_i (x_i -\bar{x})^2} \sqrt{ \sum_i (y_i -\bar{y})^2}  }</math>

For <math>M=1</math> this reduces to Moran's <math>I</math>. For larger values of <math>M</math> the diagonals of <math>I</math> are the Moran indices for each of the variables and the off-diagonals give the corresponding Wartenberg correlation coefficients. <math>I</math> is an example of a Mantel statistic and so its significance can be evaluated using the [[Mantel test]].<ref>{{cite book
|last1 = Dale
|first1 = Mark R. T.
|last2 = Fortin
|first2 = Marie-Josée
|date = 2014
|title = Spatial Analysis: A Guide For Ecologists
|publisher=Cambridge University Press
|page=428
|isbn=978-0-521-14350-9
}}</ref>

== Criticisms ==
Lee<ref>{{Cite journal
 | doi = 10.1007/s101090100064
 | first1 = Sang-Il
 | last1 = Lee
 | year = 2001
 | title =Developing a bivariate spatial association measure: an integration of Pearson's r and Moran's I.
 | journal = Journal of Geographical Systems
 | volume = 3
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 369–385
| bibcode = 2001JGS.....3..369L
 }}</ref> points out some problems with this coefficient namely:
* There is only one factor of <math>W</math> in the numerator, so the comparison is between the raw <math>x</math> data and the spatially averaged <math>y</math> data.
* <math>I_{xy} \neq I_{yx}</math> for non-symmetric spatial weight matrices.
He suggests an [[Lee's L|alternative coefficient]] which has two factors of <math>W</math> in the numerator and is symmetric for any weight matrix.
